client: I've been really stressed out lately because of my business finances — I got hit with this unexpected tax bill last week and it completely threw me off. I thought I had things somewhat under control, but now I'm not so sure, and the anxiety is just constant. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because what I really need is the money to pay these bills, not someone to chat with about my feelings.
therapist: That makes complete sense — you're facing a very real, concrete problem, and it can feel like talking is just a detour from solving it. I hear your skepticism, and I want to acknowledge that the stress you're carrying right now is genuinely heavy, not just a perception to be reframed away. That said, I'm curious — when you say the anxiety is *constant*, what does that feel like in your day-to-day, and is it getting in the way of the clear-headed thinking you'd need to actually tackle this situation?

client: Yeah, it really is constant — like, I wake up at 3am running through worst-case scenarios about money, and then I spend the whole day distracted and exhausted because I barely slept. I'll sit down to actually look at my budget or research options, and my mind just goes blank or I start spiraling into "what's the point, it's already too late." So yeah, I guess you're right that it's getting in the way, but knowing that doesn't really make it easier to just... stop doing it.
therapist: You've just identified something really important — the anxiety isn't just an uncomfortable feeling running alongside the problem, it's actually *blocking* you from the very actions that could help you solve it. That thought "what's the point, it's already too late" is worth paying attention to, because it sounds like it shows up right at the moment you're trying to take action, almost like a circuit breaker shutting things down. I'm wondering — when that thought appears, does it feel like an undeniable fact, or is there a part of you that recognizes it might not be the whole truth?

client: Honestly, in the moment it feels completely like a fact — like, my brain just accepts it as truth and shuts everything down before I even have a chance to think otherwise. But sitting here now, talking about it, I can kind of see that maybe it's not totally true, like there's a small part of me that knows I'm probably exaggerating how hopeless the situation is. It's just that that small part feels really far away when the anxiety kicks in, like I can hear it but I can't actually reach it.
therapist: What you just described is actually a really significant insight — that wiser part of you *exists*, even if anxiety keeps it at arm's length in those hard moments. In CBT we'd call that "what's the point, it's already too late" an automatic thought, and the fact that you can already see some distance between it and reality, even just right now, means you have more agency here than it feels like at 3am. I'm curious — if that calmer, wiser part of you *could* speak up in one of those moments, what do you think it might say about your situation?

client: I mean... I think that wiser part of me would probably say something like, "you're not actually as alone as you feel right now, and the fact that you're still here, still trying, still showing up to therapy, that counts for something." But honestly, Luna, it feels almost embarrassing to even say that out loud, like I'm just telling myself what I want to hear. And at 3am when my chest is tight and I'm lying there replaying everything I did wrong that day, that voice feels so far away it might as well not exist.
therapist: What you just said doesn't sound like wishful thinking to me — it sounds like genuine self-knowledge, and the fact that it feels embarrassing to claim it says a lot about how hard you've been on yourself through all of this. That 3am version of you is exhausted, flooded with stress hormones, and replaying mistakes — it's not a fair fight between anxiety and wisdom in that state, which is why we'd want to build some kind of bridge to that wiser voice *before* you're in the thick of it. I'm wondering — would you be open to trying something small, like writing down that exact thing you just said, so it's somewhere concrete you can reach for when that chest tightness wakes you up at night?

client: I mean... maybe. I guess I'm just not sure I'd actually reach for it in that moment — like, when I'm already spiraling at 3am, the last thing I want to do is turn on a light and find a piece of paper. It also feels a little weird to write something nice about myself, like I'd be setting myself up to feel even more pathetic if it doesn't work.
therapist: That's really honest, and it's worth taking seriously — there's no point in a plan that doesn't fit how you actually function at 3am. And I notice that thought too: "if it doesn't work, I'll feel even more pathetic" — that's anxiety protecting itself, making sure you don't even try anything that might loosen its grip. What if we thought of it less as writing something nice about yourself, and more as just leaving a note from *right now you* — the one who can see a little more clearly — to *3am you*, the way you might leave a note for a friend who's struggling?

client: I kind of like the idea of framing it as a note to a friend, because when I think about it that way it doesn't feel as loaded. But honestly, I'm not sure what "right now me" even has to offer, because right now I still feel pretty lost too, just... less acutely. What if I sit down to write it and nothing comes out, or what comes out sounds hollow even to me?
therapist: "Less acutely lost" is actually more than you're giving yourself credit for — that's a real difference, and it's exactly the kind of clarity that evaporates at 3am, which makes it worth capturing even imperfectly. And if what comes out feels hollow, that's okay — you're not writing a motivational poster, you're just leaving a small breadcrumb for yourself, and even a sentence like "this feels unbearable right now, but earlier today I could see it wasn't the whole truth" is enough. What do you think would feel like a low-enough bar that the writing itself wouldn't become another thing to fail at?

client: I like how you framed that, the breadcrumb thing. It takes some of the pressure off, like I don't have to solve anything or even feel better, just... leave a note for the version of me who's drowning at 3am. I think the bar would have to be something like, just open the notes app and type one sentence, even if it's just "today wasn't completely terrible" — anything more and I'll probably talk myself out of starting.
therapist: That's a perfect bar — genuinely, one sentence in a notes app is something exhausted, anxious 3am you can actually reach for without turning on a light or doing anything that feels like "trying too hard." And "today wasn't completely terrible" might sound small, but it's actually a direct counter to that automatic thought that says it's already too late — it's evidence, collected by you, for you. I'm curious — is there a moment in the next day or two that feels realistic to try this, even just once, so it doesn't stay as an idea but becomes something you've actually done?

client: I mean... maybe tonight, actually. I've been lying awake the last few nights anyway, so it's not like I'd be doing something out of the ordinary. I guess my worry is that I'll do it once and then forget about it, or it'll feel pointless after a few days and I'll just stop, which kind of feels like failing all over again.
therapist: It says a lot that you're willing to try it tonight, and I want to gently point out that you just anticipated failing at something that hasn't even started yet — which is that same protective anxiety trying to talk you out of trying before you begin. What if we reframed it so that doing it *once* is already a complete success, not a trial run that has to become a habit to count, because one breadcrumb left for 3am you is genuinely worth something regardless of what happens after? And if it does fade after a few days, that's not failure — that's just information about what you need next, and we can work with that together.

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that one time could actually count for something. But there's this voice in my head that's already saying "yeah, but you'll probably forget to do it, or you'll do it and it won't help, and then what?" It's like even before I've tried, I'm already writing the story of how it falls apart.
therapist: You just described that pattern so clearly and precisely — you're not just anxious about the tax bill anymore, you're anxious about the anxiety not going away, which is exhausting in its own right. That voice writing the failure story in advance is trying to protect you from disappointment, but it's also stealing the experience before you've even had it. What would it feel like to just let tonight be an experiment with no predetermined ending — not a test you can pass or fail, just something you're trying once to see what happens?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe I could just treat tonight like a neutral experiment, but honestly it feels kind of impossible. Like, how do I just switch off the part of my brain that's already decided it's going to be awkward and that I'll come home feeling worse than before? I want to try, I really do, but I don't trust that I can actually pull it off in the moment when the anxiety hits.
therapist: You don't have to switch that part off — it's going to be there, and that's okay, because the goal tonight isn't to feel confident or calm, it's just to open your notes app and type one sentence while that voice is still running in the background. The fact that you're saying "I want to try, I really do" matters more than you might realize — that's not nothing, that's the wiser part of you showing up even now, even through all the doubt. What would it mean to you, just sitting here in this moment, if you did it tonight and that critical voice turned out to be wrong?
